the Eocene–early Oligocene climate change in the North American Great Plains and the Cypress Hills was a global phenomenon, with the exception of a larger increase in temperature seasonally in the Cypress Hills.
the climate of the Eocene–early Oligocene of North America was relatively stable, with only minor changes in mean annual precipitation and a large increase in mean annual temperature seasonality.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Eocene– Oligocene transition in North America was characterized by a large increase in the amplitude of temperature seasonality, which was accompanied by a drop in atmospheric CO 2 and a slight decrease in aridity.

the Eocene– Oligocene transition in Saskatchewan was characterized by the establishment of a more seasonal climate with drier and cooler winters and no change in precipitation and temperature seasonality.
the Eocene– Oligocene climate cooling in North American mid-latitudes was not accompanied by a significant change in the latitudinal gradient of local water δ 13 C or δ 18 O.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stable isotope analyses of fossil teeth can be used to reconstruct paleoenvironments at high latitudes, which are poorly represented by other proxy data, such as marine sediments.
the Eocene–early Oligocene climate change was not a simple bipolar cooling, but a much more complex phenomenon that involved large latitudinal gradients in temperature seasonality.
